title: Frozen Dataclasses

glossary.definition: An object whose state or data cannot be changed or modified after it is created. Example: `frozenset`([1, 2])
An object that has a fixed value that never changes during its lifetime, allowing it to be used as a dict key or set item. Example: hash('text')

overview.what:
A frozen dataclass is a dataclass where instances cannot be modified after initialization.

You create it by passing `frozen=True` to the @dataclass decorator:

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Point:
      x: int
      y: int

This makes the class immutable, similar to a `tuple`. It automatically generates a __hash__ method, allowing instances to be used as dict keys or stored in a set.

Mental model: A frozen dataclass is a read-only container; once you lock it, any attempt to change its fields raises a `FrozenInstanceError`.

  p = Point(1, 2)
  p.x = 3  # Raises FrozenInstanceError

The `frozen=True` parameter only prevents reassignment of the fields. It does not make the object deeply immutable.

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Group:
      members: list[str]

  g = Group(['Alice'])
  g.members.append('Bob')  # Works! The list itself mutated

If a field contains a mutable object like a list or dict, you can still mutate that inner object.
overview.why:
Immutability prevents accidental state changes in data passed around your application.

It also makes objects hashable, meaning they can be used as keys in a dict or elements in a set.

why_learning_this: You can safely pass data objects around without worrying about other functions mutating them.
You can use complex data structures as keys in a dict or elements in a set.

common_mistakes.title: Mutating internal lists
common_mistakes.explanation: The `frozen=True` parameter only applies to the attributes directly on the class. If a field is a mutable object like a list, you can still mutate the list itself.

common_mistakes.title: Manual __hash__ conflicts
common_mistakes.explanation: Providing a custom __hash__ or __eq__ method can conflict with the one generated by `frozen=True`, leading to unexpected equality behaviors.

recall_questions.q: How do you make a dataclass immutable?
recall_questions.answer: By passing the `frozen=True` argument to the @dataclass decorator. This makes the generated class immutable.

recall_questions.q: What additional magic method does `frozen=True` automatically generate?
recall_questions.answer: It automatically generates a __hash__ method, making the instance hashable if its fields are also hashable.

recall_questions.q: Why would you want to make a dataclass frozen?
recall_questions.answer: To prevent accidental state mutation, keeping data safe from unintended changes. It also allows the instances to be used as dict keys or in a set.

recall_questions.q: Does `frozen=True` make the dataclass deeply immutable?
recall_questions.answer: No, it only prevents reassignment of the fields. If a field contains a mutable object like a list, that internal object can still be mutated.

understanding_checks.question: What is printed when this code is executed?
understanding_checks.why:
Because `frozen=True` prevents reassignment of fields after the object is created.

Attempting to assign c.retries = 5 raises a FrozenInstanceError.

understanding_checks.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Team:
    name: str
    members: List[str]

t = Team('A', ['Alice'])
t.members.append('Bob')
print(len(t.members))
understanding_checks.question: What is printed when this code is executed?
understanding_checks.why:
Frozen dataclasses only prevent reassignment of the attribute, such as `t.members` = [...].

They do not make the underlying mutable objects, like a list, immutable. The list itself can still be modified.

code_walkthrough.focus: points_set = {p1, p2} shows that frozen dataclasses are hashable and equal instances are deduplicated.

aha_moment.prediction: Will this successfully retrieve the value 42, or raise a KeyError because they are different objects?
aha_moment.common_guess: KeyError, because they are two different instances in memory.
aha_moment.why:
It prints 42.

The `frozen=True` parameter generates a __hash__ method based on the fields.

Since both instances have identical fields, they hash to the same value and __eq__ evaluates to True, allowing them to act as identical dict keys.

challenge.title: Using Dataclasses in Sets
challenge.prompt: Create a frozen dataclass UserIdentifier with two str fields: email and `tenant_id`. Then, initialize a set containing two identical instances of UserIdentifier and print the len of the set.
